full_prose_under_review.title: Schedule II Partial Fills and the Massachusetts 30-Day Ceiling
full_prose_under_review.subtopic: Choosing the pathway, the clock, the record and the actor
learning_objectives: Distinguish a prohibited refill from a lawful remainder of a partial fill.
Choose the federal remainder clock by identifying which partial-fill pathway the facts trigger.
Apply the Massachusetts 30-day issue-date ceiling on top of whichever federal clock the pathway supplies.
Apply the Massachusetts five-day limit using the trigger the regulation actually states.
State what each actor must specify or record in each pathway.

orientation.text: A Schedule II prescription cannot be refilled. That single sentence causes most of the confusion in this area, because a partial fill looks like a refill from the counter: the patient comes back and leaves with more drug. The difference is that a refill is a fresh authorisation to dispense the full quantity again, while the remainder of a partial fill is the unfilled balance of the one quantity the prescriber already authorised. Nothing is created; something already authorised is completed. Getting that distinction right is what lets the rest of the area make sense.

Federal law then supplies three separate partial-fill pathways, and each carries its own clock. Where the pharmacy simply could not supply the full quantity, the remainder may be filled within 72 hours of the first partial filling, after which the prescriber must be notified and no further quantity may go out without a new prescription. Where the patient or the prescriber asked for a partial fill, the remainder runs to 30 days after the prescription was written -- except that an emergency oral prescription collapses that to 72 hours from issue. Where the patient is in a long-term care facility or has a documented terminal illness, partial filling may continue for up to 60 days from issue unless the medication is discontinued sooner. The first question on any partial-fill fact pattern is therefore never 'how long', it is 'which pathway', because the pathway picks the clock.

Massachusetts then puts a ceiling over all of it. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(a) provides without qualification that a written or electronic Schedule II prescription becomes invalid 30 days after the date of issuance. There is no long-term care or terminal-illness carve-out from that sentence. So the federal 60-day figure, which is a real and correctly stated federal outer limit, cannot be worked in Massachusetts past day 30: on day 31 there is no longer a valid prescription for the pathway to operate on. A federal outer limit is a ceiling on federal authority. It is never a grant of state validity, and the 60-day answer belongs only to a question that asks what federal law alone permits.

Massachusetts also has its own partial-fill scheme, and it appears twice with two different triggers. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d3/4) makes the lesser-quantity dispensing mandatory on patient request, keeps the remainder at the same pharmacy, requires a patient-record notation, closes the remainder at 30 days from issue, and imposes a five-day limit on the INITIAL partial dispensing of a prescription filled pursuant to subsection (d) or (d1/2). 105 CMR 721.055(A) states the same five-day limit but triggers it off something a pharmacist can actually see: whether the prescriber's address ON THE PRESCRIPTION is outside the Commonwealth, counted in calendar days. The regulation is the operational form of the statute's rule, and it is the one that decides the question at the counter.

Finally the records, which are where the actors separate. On the stock-shortage pathway the pharmacist notes the quantity supplied. On the request-based pathway the practitioner has work to do first -- specifying the quantity for each partial filling, and capping what a patient may later ask for -- before the pharmacist's notation identifies who requested the fill and when. On the long-term care and terminal-illness pathway the notation is not clerical at all: a partially filled prescription that does not carry 'terminally ill' or 'LTCF patient' is deemed by the regulation to have been filled in violation of the Act. Massachusetts adds its own patient-record notation, and requires a Schedule II opioid prescription to carry on its face the notation that the patient may request less than the full quantity.

worked_examples.scenario: A Massachusetts written oxycodone prescription for an LTCF resident is issued on 1 March and partially filled on 5 March under the federal long-term care pathway. On 12 April the facility asks for a further partial quantity. The prescription has not been discontinued and quantity remains authorised. Federal law would still allow it. May you dispense?
steps: Confirm the federal pathway is genuinely open. 12 April is day 42 from issue, inside the 60-day outer limit, and the medication has not been discontinued, so federal law does not stop you.
Now apply the Massachusetts ceiling. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(a) invalidates a written or electronic Schedule II prescription 30 days after the date of issuance, without qualification.
Day 30 from 1 March is 31 March. The prescription became invalid on 31 March, eleven days before the request.

Ask what the federal 60-day figure actually is. It is an outer limit on that federal pathway, not a grant of Massachusetts validity, so it cannot revive a prescription the state has already invalidated.
worked_examples.resolution: No. The prescription is dead in Massachusetts and a further partial dispensing would be made on an invalid prescription. The error this invites is answering 60 days because the question mentions an LTCF resident; 60 days is the right answer only where the question asks what federal law alone permits.

worked_examples.scenario: A patient presents a Schedule II prescription written by a Rhode Island prescriber whose address is printed on the prescription, issued six days ago, and asks for only part of the quantity. Your colleague says the five-day limit does not apply because nobody has established which statutory subsection the prescription came in under.
steps: Read the regulation rather than the statute. 105 CMR 721.055(A) attaches the five-day limit where the prescription was issued by a prescriber from a location other than the Commonwealth, as indicated by the address of the prescriber on the prescription.
That test is satisfied on its face here: the address printed on the prescription is out of state. No subsection adjudication is required.
Count in calendar days from the prescription issue date, which is what the regulation specifies. Six days is outside the limit.
Note what the limit governs. It is the deadline for presenting the prescription for INITIAL partial fill, not the general validity of the prescription.
worked_examples.resolution: The initial partial fill can no longer be made on this prescription. The colleague's test is the statute's; the regulation supplies an address-based trigger that the pharmacist can apply from the face of the prescription, and it is the operative one at the counter.

worked_examples.scenario: A prescriber writes a Schedule II prescription for 60 tablets and specifies on its face that it is to be partially filled in three dispensings of 20. After the first 20 are dispensed, the patient telephones and asks for 30 next time because they are going away. Your technician says a patient may request any quantity they like.
steps: Confirm the request route is valid. A patient may request a partial fill in person, in writing if signed, or by telephone, so the telephone call is not the problem.
Check whether the practitioner has already specified quantities. Here they specified 20 per filling on the face of the prescription under 21 CFR 1306.13(b)(3).
Apply the cap. Where the practitioner has requested partial filling in that way, the patient may not request a partial filling in an amount greater than the practitioner specified.
Keep the running total in view: across all partial fillings the total dispensed may not exceed the total quantity prescribed.
Record the request properly: the patient requested a partial fill on a stated date, with the quantity dispensed.
worked_examples.resolution: You may dispense up to 20, not 30. Going to 30 would need the prescriber to change the specification. The technician's rule is right for a prescription the practitioner left unspecified and wrong for this one.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Three federal partial-fill pathways, three clocks: stock shortage ______; requested partial fill ______; LTCF or terminal illness ______.
retrieval_prompts.answer: 72 hours from the first partial filling; 30 days from when the prescription was written (72 hours from issue if it was an emergency oral prescription); up to 60 days from the issue date.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Why can a Massachusetts LTCF partial fill not run to 60 days?
retrieval_prompts.answer: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(a) invalidates a written or electronic Schedule II prescription 30 days after issuance with no LTCF or terminal-illness carve-out, and a federal outer limit is not a grant of state validity.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: True or false: the Massachusetts five-day partial-fill limit applies only once you have established that the prescription was filled under s. 18(d) or s. 18(d1/2).
retrieval_prompts.answer: False. 105 CMR 721.055(A) triggers it off the prescriber's address as it appears on the prescription, counted in calendar days.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A partially filled LTCF prescription does not carry the words 'LTCF patient' or 'terminally ill'. What follows?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The regulation deems it to have been filled in violation of the Act.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What four things must be recorded for EACH partial filling on the LTCF or terminal-illness pathway?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The date of the partial filling, the quantity dispensed, the remaining quantity authorised to be dispensed, and the identification of the dispensing pharmacist.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Where the practitioner has already specified per-fill quantities, may the patient request a larger partial fill?
retrieval_prompts.answer: No. A patient, a minor's parent or legal guardian, or an adult patient's named caregiver may not request more than the practitioner specified.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: In Massachusetts, is dispensing a lesser quantity on patient request permitted or required?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Required. The pharmacist shall dispense the lesser quantity if the patient requests it.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Where must the Schedule II opioid partial-fill notation appear?
retrieval_prompts.answer: On the prescription itself, under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 22(c) — not merely in the pharmacy record.

quick_review.text: A Schedule II prescription may not be refilled; dispensing a lawful unfilled remainder of a partial fill is not a refill.

Federal law supplies three partial-fill pathways with three different remainder clocks: 72 hours when the pharmacy could not supply the full quantity, 30 days from the writing date when the patient or prescriber requested the partial fill, and up to 60 days from issue for an LTCF resident or a terminally ill patient.

In Massachusetts a written or electronic Schedule II prescription becomes invalid 30 days after the date of issuance under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(a), so no federal pathway can be worked past day 30 on that prescription.

M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d3/4) makes the lesser-quantity dispensing mandatory on patient request, keeps the remaining portion at the same pharmacy, requires a patient-record notation of the partial fill and quantity, and requires the remaining portion to be filled not later than 30 days after the prescription issue date.

105 CMR 721.055(A) states the five-day initial partial-fill limit with an address-based trigger: it applies where the prescriber's address on the prescription is outside the Commonwealth, counted in calendar days from issue.

Every federal partial fill carries a notation duty of its own, the request-based pathway requires the practitioner to specify per-fill quantities in advance, and on the LTCF or terminal-illness pathway a partially filled prescription lacking the 'terminally ill' or 'LTCF patient' notation is deemed filled in violation of the Act.
A Massachusetts prescription for a Schedule II opioid must itself carry a notation that the patient may fill it, upon request, in an amount not exceeding the full prescribed quantity.

decision_logic.condition: The original Schedule II quantity was fully dispensed.
decision_logic.action: Do not process an additional dispensing as a refill; require a new lawful prescription unless a distinct pathway applies.

decision_logic.condition: The pharmacy could not supply the full Schedule II quantity.
decision_logic.action: Note the quantity supplied on the prescription record, then use the 72-hour remainder rule; past 72 hours notify the prescriber and obtain a new prescription for any further quantity.

decision_logic.condition: The patient or the prescriber requested a partial fill of a written or electronic Schedule II prescription and state law does not prohibit it.
decision_logic.action: Check whether the practitioner specified per-fill quantities, record the requester and the date of the request with the quantity dispensed, and complete any remainder no later than 30 days after the prescription was written.

decision_logic.condition: The patient or prescriber requested a partial fill of an emergency oral Schedule II prescription.
decision_logic.action: Complete any remainder no later than 72 hours after the prescription was issued; the ordinary 30-day request-based period does not reach an emergency oral prescription.

decision_logic.condition: The Schedule II prescription is for an LTCF resident or a patient with a documented terminal illness.
decision_logic.action: Record 'LTCF patient' or 'terminally ill' on the prescription before partially filling it, contact the practitioner first if terminal status is uncertain, and log the date, quantity dispensed, remaining quantity authorised and dispensing pharmacist for each partial filling.

decision_logic.condition: The prescriber's address printed on a Schedule II prescription is outside Massachusetts.
decision_logic.action: The prescription must be presented for initial partial fill not later than five calendar days after its issue date.

decision_logic.condition: The federal pathway you selected would allow a further partial dispensing more than 30 days after the Massachusetts written or electronic Schedule II prescription was issued.
decision_logic.action: Stop. The prescription is already invalid in Massachusetts under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(a); the federal outer limit is a ceiling on federal authority and does not extend Massachusetts validity.

decision_logic.condition: A Massachusetts patient requests a lesser quantity of a Schedule II prescription.
decision_logic.action: Dispense the lesser quantity, note the partial fill and quantity in the patient record accessible to the prescriber on request, keep any remainder at the same pharmacy, and fill it not later than 30 days after the issue date.

ma_vs_federal.text: 21 CFR 1306.13(c) allows LTCF and terminal-illness Schedule II partial fills for up to 60 days from issue, but M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(a) invalidates the written or electronic prescription 30 days after issuance. Both apply, so in Massachusetts the working outer limit is 30 days and the federal 60-day figure answers only a question about federal law alone.

Federal patient-requested partial filling is permissive and asks only that the partial fill not be prohibited by state law; M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d3/4) goes further and makes the lesser-quantity dispensing mandatory on patient request while adding same-pharmacy, patient-record and issue-date conditions.
Partial-fill notation is not a Massachusetts-only duty: 21 CFR 1306.13(a) and (b)(5) impose federal notation and dispensing-record duties that run alongside the Massachusetts patient-record notation.

exceptions.text: The 72-hour remainder rule is tied to the pharmacy's inability to supply the full quantity and is not a substitute for the request-based pathway.

The request-based 30-day remainder period carries its own emergency-oral exception: the remainder of a partially filled emergency oral Schedule II prescription must be filled no later than 72 hours after the prescription is issued.
The 60-day LTCF and terminal-illness period is an outer limit on that federal pathway, not an extension of any state validity period, and it ends earlier if the medication is discontinued.

The five-day initial partial-dispensing limit in M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d3/4) reaches only a prescription filled under subsection (d) or (d1/2) -- respectively a nonnarcotic Schedule II prescription from an out-of-state practitioner and a narcotic Schedule II prescription from a practitioner registered in Maine or a state contiguous with the commonwealth -- and not every patient-requested partial fill. The conditions those two subsections place on the underlying prescription are the subject of the out-of-state pathway, not of this section.

Where the practitioner has specified per-fill quantities in advance, a patient-side request may not exceed them, and no pathway permits the total across all partial fillings to exceed the total quantity prescribed.

timing_deadlines.timeframe: Within 72 hours of the first partial filling
timing_deadlines.consequence: Otherwise notify the prescriber; no further quantity may be supplied beyond 72 hours without a new prescription.

timing_deadlines.event: Request-based Schedule II remainder, written or electronic prescription
timing_deadlines.timeframe: No later than 30 days after the prescription was written
timing_deadlines.consequence: The remaining portion cannot be dispensed after the deadline.

timing_deadlines.event: Request-based Schedule II remainder, emergency oral prescription
timing_deadlines.timeframe: No later than 72 hours after the prescription is issued
timing_deadlines.consequence: The emergency oral remainder cannot use the ordinary 30-day request-based period.

timing_deadlines.event: LTCF or terminal-illness Schedule II partial fills, federal ceiling
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Up to 60 days from the issue date unless discontinued sooner
timing_deadlines.consequence: The federal outer limit on the pathway; correct only where the question asks what federal law alone permits.

timing_deadlines.event: Massachusetts written or electronic Schedule II prescription, including one being partially filled on the LTCF or terminal-illness pathway
timing_deadlines.timeframe: 30 days after the date of issuance
timing_deadlines.consequence: The prescription becomes invalid, so further partial dispensing must stop at day 30 even though federal law would have allowed 60.

timing_deadlines.event: Initial partial fill where the prescriber's address on the prescription is outside Massachusetts
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Not later than 5 calendar days after the prescription issue date
timing_deadlines.consequence: The prescription can no longer be presented for an initial partial fill.

timing_deadlines.event: Massachusetts remaining portion after a patient-requested partial fill
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Not later than 30 days after the prescription issue date
timing_deadlines.consequence: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d3/4) closes the remainder at the same point the general validity rule closes the prescription.

forms_records.text: On the stock-shortage pathway the pharmacist notes the quantity supplied on the face of the written prescription, in the written record of the emergency oral prescription, or in the electronic prescription record.

On the request-based pathway the practitioner specifies the quantity for each partial filling in advance, and the pharmacist's notation then identifies who requested the partial fill and when: a practitioner request made in consultation is noted as 'Authorized by Practitioner to Partial Fill' with the practitioner's name, the date and time of the discussion and the pharmacist's initials, and a patient, guardian or named caregiver request is noted as that person having requested the partial fill on a stated date, with the quantity dispensed.

Each request-based partial filling also generates a dispensing record carrying the date, the name or initials of the person who dispensed, and the elements 21 CFR 1306.22(c) requires for Schedule III and IV refills; for an electronic prescription that information must be linked to the electronic prescription record.

On the LTCF or terminal-illness pathway the pharmacist records 'terminally ill' or 'LTCF patient' on the prescription itself, and for each partial filling records the date, the quantity dispensed, the remaining quantity authorised and the dispensing pharmacist's identification.

Massachusetts adds a notation of each partial dispensing and its quantity in the pharmacy patient record, accessible to the prescribing practitioner on request, whether the dispensing is the initial partial fill or the remaining portion.

A Massachusetts prescription for a Schedule II opioid must itself carry the notation under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 22(c) that the patient may fill it, upon request, in an amount not exceeding the full prescribed quantity.

role_duties.duty: Identify the factual trigger for the partial fill before selecting any deadline, because the three federal pathways carry three different clocks.
Specify the quantity to be dispensed in each partial filling where a request-based partial fill is intended, and keep the total within the quantity prescribed.
Check the Massachusetts issue-date ceiling before dispensing any remainder, since a federal pathway that is still open may sit on a prescription Massachusetts has already invalidated.
Dispense the lesser quantity when a Massachusetts patient requests a partial fill of a Schedule II prescription; that dispensing is mandatory rather than discretionary.

Contact the practitioner before partially filling where it is unclear whether the patient may be classified as terminally ill; the responsibility to assure the substance is for a terminally ill patient is shared with the prescriber.

common_traps.text: Calling every later Schedule II dispensing a refill erases the lawful partial-fill remainder distinction.
Choosing 72 hours whenever a Schedule II prescription is partial ignores who requested the partial fill and why.
Carrying the federal 60-day figure into a Massachusetts scenario dispenses a Schedule II drug on a prescription that M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(a) invalidated on day 31.
Reading the Massachusetts patient-requested partial fill as an option the pharmacist may decline turns a mandatory duty into a permission.
Looking for the statutory subsection before applying the five-day limit misses that the regulation triggers it off the prescriber's address printed on the prescription.
Treating the LTCF or terminal-illness notation as clerical overlooks that a partially filled prescription without it is deemed filled in violation of the Act.
Assuming a patient may request any partial quantity ignores the cap a practitioner's advance specification imposes.
Assuming the Schedule II opioid partial-fill notation lives in the pharmacy record misses that M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 22(c) places it on the prescription itself.

authority.name: Schedule II prescriptions may not be refilled

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Federal law prohibits refilling a Schedule II prescription; additional dispensing requires a new lawful prescription or a permitted remainder of a partial fill.
exceptions: Apply any narrower setting-specific, product-specific, or emergency exception before the general rule.

authority.name: Schedule II partial fill caused by pharmacy inability

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: When a Schedule II prescription is partially filled because the pharmacy cannot supply the full quantity, the remaining portion must generally be supplied within 72 hours or the pharmacist must notify the prescriber and obtain a new prescription for further quantity.
exceptions: Apply any narrower setting-specific, product-specific, or emergency exception before the general rule.

authority.name: Patient-requested Schedule II partial fill

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: A Schedule II prescription may be partially filled at the patient or prescriber request when state law permits, with the remaining portion dispensed no later than 30 days after the prescription was written unless a shorter applicable limit controls.
exceptions: Apply any narrower setting-specific, product-specific, or emergency exception before the general rule.

authority.name: Electronic Code of Federal Regulations

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Federal law permits Schedule II prescriptions for LTCF residents or terminally ill patients to be partially filled under a special documentation framework for up to 60 days from issue unless the prescription is discontinued sooner.

authority.name: Partial filling, stock shortage notation
Request-based partial filling, conditions and records

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under 21 CFR 1306.13(a) the stock-shortage partial fill is permissible only if the pharmacist MAKES A NOTATION OF THE QUANTITY SUPPLIED on the face of the written prescription, in the written record of the emergency oral prescription, or in the electronic prescription record. The REQUEST-BASED pathway in 1306.13(b) allocates duties to both actors. Its general conditions in (b)(1) are conjunctive: the partial fill is not prohibited by State law; the prescription is written and filled in accordance with the Act, the chapter and State law; the partial fill is requested by the PATIENT, by one acting on the patient's behalf (a parent or legal guardian of a minor, or a caregiver of an adult patient named in a medical power of attorney), or by the PRACTITIONER who wrote the prescription; and THE TOTAL QUANTITY DISPENSED IN ALL PARTIAL FILLINGS DOES NOT EXCEED THE TOTAL QUANTITY PRESCRIBED. Under (b)(3), a practitioner who wants the prescription partially filled MUST SPECIFY THE QUANTITY TO BE DISPENSED IN EACH PARTIAL FILLING on the face of the written prescription, in the written record of the emergency oral prescription, or in the electronic record; after consultation with a pharmacist the practitioner may authorize a partial fill at a later date, but the prescription must still be filled not later than 30 days after it was written, or 72 hours for an emergency oral prescription. Under (b)(4) a request may be made in person, in writing if signed by the requester, or by telephone; and WHERE THE PRACTITIONER HAS ALREADY SPECIFIED QUANTITIES UNDER (b)(3), the patient, guardian or named caregiver MAY NOT REQUEST A PARTIAL FILLING GREATER THAN THE AMOUNT THE PRACTITIONER SPECIFIED. Under (b)(5) the pharmacist's notation differs by requester: a practitioner request made in consultation is noted as 'Authorized by Practitioner to Partial Fill' with the practitioner's name, the date and time of the discussion and the pharmacist's initials, while a patient, guardian or caregiver request is noted as that named person having requested the partial fill on a stated date, together with the quantity dispensed. Every request-based partial filling also generates a dispensing record carrying the date, the name or initials of the dispenser, and the other elements 21 CFR 1306.22(c) requires for Schedule III and IV refills; for electronic prescriptions that information must be LINKED to the electronic prescription record.
exceptions: The stock-shortage notation under 1306.13(a) is only the quantity supplied; the fuller request-based notations belong to 1306.13(b)(5).
A consultation-authorized partial fill adds the 'Authorized by Practitioner to Partial Fill' notation that a partial fill specified on the face of the prescription does not require.
Where the practitioner has specified per-fill quantities, a patient-side request cannot exceed them.
The remaining-portion period is 30 days from writing, except 72 hours where the prescription was an emergency oral one.

authority.name: Partial filling for LTCF residents and terminally ill patients

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under 21 CFR 1306.13(c) the pharmacist MUST RECORD ON THE PRESCRIPTION whether the patient is 'terminally ill' or an 'LTCF patient', and A PARTIALLY FILLED PRESCRIPTION THAT DOES NOT CARRY THAT NOTATION SHALL BE DEEMED TO HAVE BEEN FILLED IN VIOLATION OF THE ACT. If there is any question whether a patient may be classified as terminally ill the pharmacist must CONTACT THE PRACTITIONER BEFORE partially filling, and pharmacist and prescribing practitioner carry a CORRESPONDING RESPONSIBILITY to assure the substance is for a terminally ill patient. For EACH partial filling the dispensing pharmacist shall record, on the back of the prescription or on another appropriate uniformly maintained and readily retrievable record, the DATE of the partial filling, the QUANTITY DISPENSED, the REMAINING QUANTITY AUTHORIZED to be dispensed, and the IDENTIFICATION OF THE DISPENSING PHARMACIST. The total dispensed in all partial fillings must not exceed the total quantity prescribed.
exceptions: The notation duty is not a formality: 21 CFR 1306.13(c) deems a partially filled prescription without it filled in violation of the Act.
Where terminal-illness status is uncertain the practitioner must be contacted before the partial fill, not after it.

authority.name: Massachusetts Schedule II prescription validity

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: A Massachusetts written or electronic Schedule II prescription becomes invalid 30 days after its issue date.
exceptions: Apply any narrower setting-specific, product-specific, or emergency exception before the general rule.

authority.name: Massachusetts General Laws
authority.section: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d3/4), read with s. 18(d) and s. 18(d1/2)

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d3/4) a pharmacist filling a Schedule II prescription SHALL, if requested by the patient, dispense a lesser quantity; ONLY THE SAME PHARMACY that dispensed the lesser quantity may dispense the remaining portion; a notation of the partial fill and quantity goes in the patient record, accessible to the prescriber on request; and the remaining portion MUST BE FILLED NOT LATER THAN 30 DAYS AFTER THE PRESCRIPTION ISSUE DATE. The separate FIVE-DAY limit on the INITIAL partial dispensing applies only to a prescription FILLED PURSUANT TO SUBSECTION (d) OR (d1/2) -- respectively a nonnarcotic Schedule II prescription issued by an out-of-state practitioner, and a narcotic Schedule II prescription issued by a practitioner registered in Maine or a state contiguous with the commonwealth.

authority.name: Contents of prescription written by practitioner

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 22(c) any prescription issued by a practitioner for an OPIOID substance contained in Schedule II SHALL INCLUDE A NOTATION on the prescription that the patient may fill it, upon request, in compliance with M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d3/4) in an amount NOT TO EXCEED THE FULL PRESCRIBED QUANTITY. The notation is a prescription-content duty on the prescriber that accompanies the patient's statutory right to receive a lesser quantity on request.
exceptions: The notation duty reaches prescriptions for opioid substances in Schedule II; it is not a general notation requirement for every controlled-substance prescription.

authority.name: Partial fill prescriptions

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: 105 CMR 721.055(A) states the Massachusetts patient-requested partial fill as a duty: a pharmacist filling a Prescription for a schedule II controlled substance SHALL, IF REQUESTED BY THE PATIENT, dispense the substance in a lesser quantity than indicated, pursuant to M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d3/4). It then supplies the operative trigger for the five-day limit: IF THE PRESCRIPTION WAS ISSUED BY A PRESCRIBER FROM A LOCATION OTHER THAN THE COMMONWEALTH, AS INDICATED BY THE ADDRESS OF THE PRESCRIBER ON THE PRESCRIPTION, the Prescription MUST BE PRESENTED FOR INITIAL PARTIAL FILL NOT LATER THAN FIVE CALENDAR DAYS after the Prescription issue date. That is a different test from the statute's 'filled pursuant to subsection (d) or (d1/2)': the pharmacist reads the address on the face of the prescription rather than adjudicating which statutory subsection the prescription travelled under, and the count is expressly in CALENDAR days. Under 721.055(B) the remaining portion may be filled on patient request provided only the same pharmacy that dispensed the lesser quantity dispenses it and it is filled not later than 30 days after the issue date, and under 721.055(C) the pharmacist or designee makes a notation in the patient record, accessible to the prescribing practitioner on request, of the partial fill and the quantity dispensed.
exceptions: The five-calendar-day limit attaches only where the prescriber's address on the prescription is outside the Commonwealth.

full_prose_under_review.title: Emergency Oral Schedule II Dispensing
full_prose_under_review.topic: Controlled prescriptions / Emergency oral Schedule II
full_prose_under_review.subtopic: The emergency gate, the record, and which follow-up clock controls
learning_objectives: Apply each sovereign's definition of an emergency situation, and notice that they are not the same test.
Trace why a Massachusetts emergency oral prescription follows the seven-business-day route and not the two-day electronic default.
Identify which follow-up period actually binds when both sovereigns reach the same prescription.
State what the pharmacist must write down, attach or annotate at each stage.
Name the consequence the regulation attaches to the pharmacist's own failure to notify the DEA.

orientation.text: Schedule II normally means a signed prescription before the drug leaves the shelf. The emergency oral pathway is the narrow exception to that, and it is built in three layers. First a gate: the prescribing practitioner must determine that this really is an emergency, and each sovereign defines that differently. Federal law asks whether immediate administration is necessary, whether no appropriate alternative treatment is available, and whether it is not reasonably possible to provide a WRITTEN prescription before dispensing. Massachusetts asks whether immediate administration is necessary and whether it is not reasonably possible to generate or transmit an ELECTRONIC prescription, or whether requiring one would delay care in a way that harms the patient. Massachusetts carries no no-alternative-treatment element at all. Both tests are the practitioner's determination, not the pharmacist's.

Once the gate is passed, the pharmacist may dispense on the oral authorization, but only the quantity adequate to treat the patient during the emergency period, and only after a reasonable effort to confirm an unknown prescriber is genuinely registered. The oral prescription is then immediately reduced to writing carrying everything a prescription normally requires except the practitioner's signature. Nothing about the emergency relaxes the rest of the prescription rules; Massachusetts says so expressly, waiving only the requirement to use an electronic prescribing system.

The third layer is the follow-up, and it is where candidates lose the question. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(c) requires an ELECTRONIC follow-up within two days whenever a practitioner prescribes a controlled substance by oral prescription, and it is tempting to read that as the shorter, stricter Massachusetts answer. It is not the route an emergency oral prescription travels. 105 CMR 721.020(A) makes a 721.070 exception the only lawful basis for a non-electronic prescription generated in the Commonwealth, and 105 CMR 721.070(A)(4) enumerates prescriptions issued or dispensed in Emergency Situations as exactly such an exception. A lawful Massachusetts emergency oral prescription is therefore always issued under an ePrescribing exception, and the regulation then says where its follow-up goes.

So Massachusetts routes it onward: 105 CMR 721.060(A) says emergency written and oral prescriptions must comply with all other prescription requirements including 105 CMR 721.070(B), and 721.070(B) sets the follow-up at not more than seven business days OR THE SHORTER PERIOD REQUIRED BY FEDERAL LAW. Federal law requires seven days. Seven calendar days expires before seven business days, so the federal period is the one that actually binds, and the Massachusetts regulation says as much in its own text rather than being overridden. The practical answer on Massachusetts facts is seven days, reached through the Massachusetts regulation rather than around it.

worked_examples.scenario: A Massachusetts prescriber telephones at 7pm on a Friday. A hospice patient needs morphine oral solution tonight; the prescriber says their e-prescribing system is down and they cannot transmit electronically before the patient needs the dose. The prescriber is not known to you. How much may you dispense, and by when must the follow-up arrive?
steps: Check the Massachusetts gate first. Immediate administration is necessary and it is not reasonably possible to transmit an electronic prescription before dispensing, so this is an Emergency Situation under 105 CMR 721.010.
Because the prescriber is not known to you, make a reasonable good faith effort to determine that the authorization came from a registered practitioner before dispensing anything.
Limit the quantity to what is adequate to treat the patient during the emergency period. Anything beyond the emergency period needs a signed prescription, not this authorization.
Immediately reduce the oral prescription to writing with every required element except the practitioner's signature.

Now pick the follow-up clock. The emergency situation is an enumerated ePrescribing exception under 105 CMR 721.070(A)(4), so the two-day electronic default in M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(c) does not apply. 105 CMR 721.060(A) routes you to 721.070(B): seven business days, or the shorter period federal law requires.
Federal law requires seven days under 21 CFR 1306.11(d)(4). Seven calendar days is shorter than seven business days, so seven days from the oral authorization is the operative deadline.
worked_examples.resolution: Dispense only the emergency-period quantity after verifying the prescriber, reduce the order to writing immediately, and expect the follow-up bearing 'Authorization for Emergency Dispensing' and the date of the oral order within seven days. Answering 'two days' here is the error the two-day rule invites.

worked_examples.scenario: Eight days have passed since you dispensed on an emergency oral Schedule II authorization. You have telephoned the prescriber's office twice and documented both calls, and no written or electronic follow-up has arrived. A colleague says the documented calls discharge your duty. Is that right?
steps: The practitioner's seven-day federal period has expired, so the follow-up is now missing rather than merely late.

Federal law places a duty on you at that point: notify the nearest office of the DEA that the practitioner failed to deliver the follow-up prescription. Chasing the prescriber is not the duty the regulation names.
Read the consequence attached to your own omission. Failure of the pharmacist to notify voids the authority conferred by 21 CFR 1306.11(d) to dispense without a written prescription.
worked_examples.resolution: The colleague is wrong. Documented calls do not substitute for the notification, and the cost of skipping it falls on the pharmacy: the emergency dispensing loses the authority it rested on, retroactively.

worked_examples.scenario: A prescriber who holds no electronic-prescribing exception telephones a Schedule IV oral prescription to your pharmacy on an ordinary Tuesday afternoon. No emergency is claimed. Your technician asks whether the seven-business-day follow-up rule you just applied to an emergency Schedule II order also covers this one.
steps: Ask which route made the oral prescription lawful. Here no emergency is claimed and the practitioner holds no exception, so this is the general oral-prescription case rather than the emergency pathway.
M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(c) therefore applies in its default form: the practitioner must cause an ELECTRONIC prescription to be delivered to the dispensing pharmacy within two days.
Note that you are not required to verify that a prescription properly falls within an ePrescribing exception or waiver; that question governs the practitioner's duty, not your authority to dispense.
worked_examples.resolution: No. The two-day electronic follow-up is the default for an oral controlled-substance prescription, and the seven-business-day route belongs to prescriptions issued under an ePrescribing exception. This is the mirror image of the emergency case and the reason the two must be told apart.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Federal law adds one element to the emergency-situation test that Massachusetts does not state at all. Name it.
retrieval_prompts.answer: That no appropriate alternative treatment is available, including a drug that is not a Schedule II controlled substance (21 CFR 290.10(b)).

retrieval_prompts.prompt: The federal emergency test turns on the impracticability of providing a ______ prescription; the Massachusetts test turns on the impracticability of an ______ prescription.
Why does the M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(c) two-day electronic follow-up NOT govern a Massachusetts emergency oral Schedule II prescription?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Because s. 20(c) diverts where the practitioner holds an ePrescribing exception, and 105 CMR 721.070(A)(4) enumerates emergency-situation prescriptions as exactly such an exception, so the prescription is always in the proviso rather than the default.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: 105 CMR 721.070(B) states the follow-up as not more than seven business days, or ______.
retrieval_prompts.answer: the shorter period that is required by federal law, which here is the seven days in 21 CFR 1306.11(d)(4).

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Two things must appear on the face of the follow-up prescription. Name both.
retrieval_prompts.answer: 'Authorization for Emergency Dispensing' and the date of the oral order.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What happens if the pharmacist does not notify the DEA when the follow-up never arrives?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The failure voids the authority conferred by 21 CFR 1306.11(d) to have dispensed without a written prescription.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A written follow-up arrives on an ordinary prescription pad. What is the format problem?
retrieval_prompts.answer: 105 CMR 721.020(F) requires a written prescription to carry the practitioner's signature and to be either transmitted by facsimile or written on a tamper-resistant form; a non-conforming format is invalid and may not be filled under 105 CMR 721.040(A).

quick_review.text: In a defined emergency a pharmacist may dispense a Schedule II substance on a practitioner's oral authorization, limited to the quantity adequate to treat the patient during the emergency period, with a reasonable effort to confirm an unknown prescriber.
The pharmacist immediately reduces the oral prescription to writing with everything 21 CFR 1306.05 requires except the practitioner's signature.

A Massachusetts emergency situation is itself an enumerated ePrescribing exception under 105 CMR 721.070(A)(4), which is why the follow-up runs on the exception route rather than the two-day electronic default.
105 CMR 721.060(B)(4) states the Massachusetts follow-up as seven business days and requires 'Authorization for Emergency Dispensing' on the face of the prescription.
Federal law requires the follow-up within seven days, and because 105 CMR 721.070(B) states its own period subject to any shorter federal one, seven calendar days is the operative deadline.
If the follow-up does not arrive, the pharmacist must notify the nearest DEA office.
A pharmacist receiving an otherwise valid written or oral prescription is not required to verify that it properly falls within an ePrescribing exception or waiver.
A written follow-up must still satisfy the Massachusetts written-format rules; a non-conforming format is invalid and may not be filled.

decision_logic.condition: A practitioner offers an oral Schedule II authorization.
decision_logic.action: Confirm the emergency gate is satisfied on the applicable test, remembering that the federal test adds a no-appropriate-alternative-treatment element and is keyed to a written prescription while the Massachusetts test is keyed to an electronic one.

decision_logic.condition: The emergency gate is satisfied and the practitioner is not known to you.
decision_logic.action: Make a reasonable good faith effort to determine the authorization came from a registered practitioner, then dispense no more than the amount adequate for the emergency period.

decision_logic.condition: You have dispensed on the oral authorization.
decision_logic.action: Immediately reduce it to writing, or enter it into a compliant electronic pharmacy system, carrying every required element except the practitioner's signature.

decision_logic.condition: You are asked how long the practitioner has to deliver the follow-up.
decision_logic.action: Do not reach for the two-day electronic default. The emergency situation is the ePrescribing exception, so 105 CMR 721.060(A) routes you to 721.070(B): seven business days or the shorter federal period, and the federal seven days is shorter.

decision_logic.condition: A written rather than electronic follow-up is used.
decision_logic.action: Check its face for 'Authorization for Emergency Dispensing' and the date of the oral order, check the written-format requirements, and attach it to the oral prescription you reduced to writing.

decision_logic.condition: The federal seven-day period has run with no follow-up delivered.
decision_logic.action: Notify the nearest DEA office of the practitioner's failure to deliver.

ma_vs_federal.text: The two definitions of an emergency situation are not the same test, so a fact pattern can satisfy one and not the other; read which sovereign the question is asking about.

Massachusetts frames the emergency as a waiver of the requirement to use an electronic prescribing system, leaving every other prescription requirement in force; federal law frames it as a narrow exception to the Schedule II written-prescription requirement.
The seven-business-day Massachusetts count is not extra time: 105 CMR 721.070(B) states it subject to any shorter period federal law requires, and 21 CFR 1306.11(d)(4)'s seven days is shorter.

exceptions.text: Dispensing beyond the emergency period is not covered by the oral authorization and requires a paper or electronic prescription signed by the practitioner.
A central fill pharmacy is not authorized to prepare a Schedule II prescription on an oral authorization from a retail pharmacist or a practitioner.
Unlike the waiver route in 105 CMR 721.070(A)(3), the emergency exception is not applied for and held by the practitioner; it attaches to the situation itself.
A mailed follow-up meets its period by the postmark rather than by the date the pharmacy receives it.

timing_deadlines.event: Federal emergency oral Schedule II follow-up
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Within 7 days after authorizing the emergency oral prescription
timing_deadlines.consequence: This is the shortest period reaching the prescription, so it is the operative deadline.

timing_deadlines.event: Massachusetts follow-up under the ePrescribing exception route
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Not more than 7 business days, or the shorter period federal law requires
timing_deadlines.consequence: 105 CMR 721.070(B) defers to the federal period rather than extending it.

timing_deadlines.event: Massachusetts emergency Schedule II follow-up stated directly
timing_deadlines.consequence: 105 CMR 721.060(B)(4) states the same period for this pathway.

timing_deadlines.timeframe: Once the federal period has run
timing_deadlines.consequence: The pharmacist must notify the nearest DEA office.

timing_deadlines.timeframe: No separate period; the consequence attaches to the omission
timing_deadlines.consequence: The authority to have dispensed without a written prescription is voided.

forms_records.text: The oral prescription is immediately reduced to writing with every element 21 CFR 1306.05 requires except the practitioner's signature.
The follow-up bears 'Authorization for Emergency Dispensing' and the date of the oral order on its face.

On receipt the pharmacist attaches a paper follow-up to the oral prescription earlier reduced to writing, and the M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(c) follow-up must itself indicate that it documents an oral prescription.
A written follow-up must carry the practitioner's signature and be either transmitted by facsimile or written on a tamper-resistant form; a non-conforming format is invalid and may not be filled.

role_duties.duty: Determine that the emergency-situation elements are met, and cause the follow-up prescription bearing the required face notations to be delivered within the period.
Limit the quantity to the emergency period, confirm an unknown prescriber, and reduce the order to writing immediately.
Notify the nearest DEA office when the follow-up is not delivered, understanding that omitting the notification voids the authority relied on to dispense.
Do not refuse an otherwise valid oral prescription for inability to confirm the practitioner's exception status; 105 CMR 721.070(C) imposes no such verification duty.

common_traps.text: Answering 'two days' on a Massachusetts emergency oral question applies the s. 20(c) default to a prescription that is always issued under an ePrescribing exception.
Answering 'seven business days' treats the Massachusetts count as extra time, when 105 CMR 721.070(B) states it subject to the shorter federal period.
Carrying the federal no-appropriate-alternative-treatment element into the Massachusetts test, or the Massachusetts delay test into the federal one, mixes two definitions that differ.
Knowing the DEA notification duty without its consequence leaves the candidate unable to say what turns on the pharmacist's omission.
Treating an emergency oral authorization as covering continued therapy overlooks that dispensing beyond the emergency period needs a signed prescription.
Refusing a prescription because the practitioner's exception status cannot be confirmed invents a verification duty the regulation does not impose on the pharmacist.

authority.name: Definition of emergency situation

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under 21 CFR 290.10, for the purpose of authorizing an ORAL prescription of a Schedule II controlled substance, an EMERGENCY SITUATION means those situations in which the prescribing practitioner determines: (a) that IMMEDIATE ADMINISTRATION of the controlled substance is necessary for proper treatment of the intended ultimate user; AND (b) that NO APPROPRIATE ALTERNATIVE TREATMENT IS AVAILABLE, including administration of a drug which is not a Schedule II controlled substance; AND (c) that it is NOT REASONABLY POSSIBLE for the prescribing practitioner to provide a WRITTEN prescription to be presented to the person dispensing the substance prior to the dispensing. All three elements are the prescribing practitioner's determination.
exceptions: The three elements are conjunctive; failing any one means the situation is not an emergency situation for this purpose.

authority.name: Emergency oral Schedule II prescription requirements

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: In a defined emergency, a pharmacist may dispense an oral Schedule II prescription only in the quantity necessary for the emergency period after immediate communication with and reasonable identification of the prescriber.
exceptions: Apply any narrower setting-specific, product-specific, or emergency exception before the general rule.

authority.name: Emergency oral Schedule II records and follow-up handling

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under 21 CFR 1306.11(d)(2) the emergency oral Schedule II prescription SHALL BE IMMEDIATELY REDUCED TO WRITING BY THE PHARMACIST and shall contain all information 21 CFR 1306.05 requires EXCEPT the prescribing individual practitioner's signature. Under 1306.11(d)(4) the follow-up prescription must bear on its face 'AUTHORIZATION FOR EMERGENCY DISPENSING' AND THE DATE OF THE ORAL ORDER; it may be delivered in person or by mail, but a mailed paper prescription MUST BE POSTMARKED WITHIN THE 7-DAY PERIOD; UPON RECEIPT the dispensing pharmacist MUST ATTACH the paper prescription to the oral emergency prescription earlier reduced to writing, and for an ELECTRONIC follow-up must ANNOTATE the electronic prescription record with the original authorization and the date of the oral order. FAILURE OF THE PHARMACIST to notify the nearest DEA office when the practitioner does not deliver the follow-up SHALL VOID THE AUTHORITY conferred by 1306.11(d) to dispense without a written prescription. Under 1306.11(d)(5) a central fill pharmacy is not authorized to prepare a Schedule II prescription on an oral authorization from a retail pharmacist or practitioner.
exceptions: A mailed follow-up satisfies the period by its postmark, not by the date the pharmacy receives it.
An electronic follow-up is annotated rather than physically attached.
The central fill prohibition in 1306.11(d)(5) removes the emergency oral route entirely for that setting.

authority.name: Follow-up after emergency oral Schedule II dispensing

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: The prescriber must deliver the required written or electronic follow-up Schedule II prescription to the pharmacy within seven days after authorizing emergency oral dispensing.
exceptions: Apply any narrower setting-specific, product-specific, or emergency exception before the general rule.

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: After an emergency oral Schedule II dispensing, if the prescribing practitioner fails to deliver the required follow-up prescription within seven days, the pharmacist must notify the DEA as required by 21 CFR 1306.11(d).
exceptions: This rule applies after a lawful emergency oral Schedule II dispensing; it is not a general rule for routine Schedule II prescriptions.

authority.name: Definition of Emergency Situation
Electronic prescription required unless an exception applies
Emergency situations enumerated as an ePrescribing exception

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: 105 CMR 721.010 defines an EMERGENCY SITUATION as (1) situations in which the prescribing practitioner intends to prescribe a controlled substance the IMMEDIATE ADMINISTRATION of which is necessary for the proper treatment of the intended ultimate user, AND EITHER (a) it is not reasonably possible for the practitioner to generate or transmit an ELECTRONIC PRESCRIPTION prior to the dispensing, OR (b) the practitioner determines the Electronic Prescription requirement would result in a DELAY THAT WOULD ADVERSELY IMPACT the patient's medical condition; or (2) any other Emergency Situation defined in Department guidance by the Commissioner under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 17. Under 105 CMR 721.020(A) every Prescription generated in the Commonwealth must be an Electronic Prescription unless it is issued under a 105 CMR 721.070 exception, and 105 CMR 721.070(A)(4) ENUMERATES 'Prescriptions issued or dispensed in Emergency Situations in accordance with 105 CMR 721.060' as exactly such an exception. A lawful Massachusetts emergency oral prescription is therefore ALWAYS issued under an ePrescribing exception, which is why 105 CMR 721.060(A) routes it to 105 CMR 721.070(B) for its follow-up rather than to the M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(c) two-day electronic default.
exceptions: Unlike 105 CMR 721.070(A)(3), the emergency exception is not applied for and held; it attaches to the situation itself.
The Commissioner may define further emergency situations in Department guidance under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 17.

authority.name: Prescribing in emergency situations

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under 105 CMR 721.060(A) an Emergency Situation waives the requirement to use an electronic prescribing system, so written and oral prescriptions may be issued, but they must comply with every other prescription requirement including 105 CMR 721.070(B). Under 721.060(B) a pharmacist may dispense a SCHEDULE II controlled substance on the written or orally transmitted authorization of a prescribing practitioner provided: the quantity is limited to the amount adequate to treat the patient during the emergency period; the prescription carries everything M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(a) requires except the practitioner's actual signature and is immediately entered into a compliant electronic pharmacy system or reduced to writing; if the practitioner is not known to the pharmacist, the pharmacist makes a reasonable good faith effort to determine the authorization came from a prescribing practitioner; WITHIN SEVEN BUSINESS DAYS the practitioner causes an electronic OR written prescription for the emergency quantity to be delivered, bearing 'Authorization for Emergency Dispensing' on its face, with a mailed written prescription postmarked within the period; and on receipt the pharmacist ATTACHES it to the orally transmitted prescription earlier reduced to writing. The pharmacist SHALL NOTIFY the nearest DEA office if the practitioner fails to deliver it.
exceptions: The emergency waiver removes the electronic-prescribing requirement only; every other prescription requirement, including 105 CMR 721.070(B), continues to apply.

authority.name: Oral prescriptions
Commissioner exceptions permitting written and oral prescriptions
Follow-up documentation for an oral prescription issued under an ePrescribing exception

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(c) a practitioner who prescribes a controlled substance by oral prescription shall cause an ELECTRONIC prescription to be delivered to the dispensing pharmacy WITHIN 2 DAYS; if the practitioner has received an electronic-prescribing exception from the commissioner under s. 23(h), the practitioner shall instead cause a WRITTEN prescription to be delivered within not more than 7 DAYS, or the shorter period required by federal law, postmarked within that period. The follow-up prescription must indicate that it documents an oral prescription, and the pharmacy attaches it to the oral prescription it reduced to writing. Under 105 CMR 721.070(B) a practitioner issuing an oral prescription for a controlled substance in SCHEDULES II THROUGH V under a 105 CMR 721.070(A) ePrescribing exception shall cause a written or electronic prescription to be delivered within not more than SEVEN BUSINESS DAYS, or the shorter period required by federal law. The s. 20(c) requirements do not apply to controlled substances in Schedule VI.
exceptions: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(c) does not apply to controlled substances in Schedule VI, although the immediate reduction to writing and the remaining validity duties still apply.
A shorter federal period controls where federal law requires one, such as the 7-day emergency oral Schedule II follow-up under 21 CFR 1306.11(d)(4).

authority.name: Standards for prescription format and security in Massachusetts
DCP Electronic Prescribing and Dispensing Manual

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Massachusetts generally requires covered prescriptions to be issued electronically subject to 105 CMR 721.070 exceptions and waivers. Schedule VI prescriptions are excepted from the state electronic-prescribing requirement under 105 CMR 721.070(A)(9). Under 105 CMR 721.070(C), a pharmacist who receives an otherwise valid written or oral prescription is not required to verify that the prescription properly falls within an electronic-prescribing exception or waiver; all other prescription and controlled-substance requirements still apply.
exceptions: Schedule VI prescriptions are excepted from the Massachusetts electronic-prescribing requirement under 105 CMR 721.070(A)(9).
Other enumerated exceptions and waivers may permit a covered prescription to be issued in written or oral form.

authority.name: Prescription formats for written prescriptions
Invalid prescriptions
Written prescription form requirement

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Where state and federal law permit a WRITTEN prescription, 105 CMR 721.020(F) requires it to be issued on a form carrying the practitioner's signature and to be EITHER transmitted via facsimile or similar technology OR written on a TAMPER-RESISTANT FORM consistent with federal requirements for Medicaid. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(i) states the same at statute level. Under 105 CMR 721.040(A) a prescription in a format that does not conform is INVALID AND SHALL NOT BE FILLED. An exception that permits a written prescription therefore removes the electronic-format mandate only; the written form requirements continue to govern the prescription the exception allows.
exceptions: The facsimile route and the tamper-resistant form route are alternatives; either satisfies 105 CMR 721.020(F)(1)-(2).
